learning_objective: 🎯 Master energy in electric fields by exploring electrostatic potential, equipotential surfaces, and how capacitors store electrical energy!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Potential is the work done to move a unit positive charge from infinity to a point in an electric field. It tells us how much 'electrical pressure' exists at a point. Formula: $V = \frac{W}{q}$.

These are imaginary surfaces where every point has the exact same electric potential. No work is done moving a charge along this surface, and electric field lines are always perfectly perpendicular to them!
A capacitor is a device that stores electrical energy and charge. Capacitance ($C$) is its storage capacity, calculated as the ratio of charge to potential difference ($C = \frac{Q}{V}$).

Dielectrics are insulating materials placed between capacitor plates. They get polarized in an electric field, which reduces the internal field and magically increases the capacitor's ability to store charge!
Building up charge on a capacitor requires work, which is stored as electrostatic potential energy. The energy stored is $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$.

fun_activity.title: ⚡ The DIY Capacitor
fun_activity.instructions: Take two flat sheets of aluminum foil (plates) and place a sheet of paper (dielectric) perfectly between them. Attach a wire to each foil. You just built a simple parallel-plate capacitor!

exam_tips: 📌 Two equipotential surfaces can NEVER intersect. If they did, there would be two different potential values at one point, which is impossible.
📌 Master the derivation for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor both with and without a dielectric slab.
📌 Remember that when capacitors are in Series, charge ($Q$) is the same. In Parallel, potential difference ($V$) is the same.
quick_recap: ⭐ Electric potential is a scalar quantity, making it easier to add up than vector electric fields.
⭐ Inserting a dielectric slab always increases the capacitance of a capacitor.
⭐ Work done moving a charge along an equipotential surface is always zero!
